entries.title: Party conflict disclosure
entries.rawBlock:
None: I am not aware of any conflict of interest in this instruction as defined by the current 
RICS Valuations Professional Standards incorporating the RICS Valuation - Global 
Professional Standards and the RICS Rules of Conduct. Should any conflict become apparent 
before completion of the inspection or report, you will be informed immediately.

current RICS Valuation Standards and the RICS Rules of Conduct. I am known to the one or 
more person connected to the property owner or the interest in the property.

entries.title: Overall opinion
entries.rawBlock:
Reasonable: I am pleased to advise you that this property is believed to be a reasonable 
proposition for purchase at a price of £390,000.00 [Three Hundred Ninety Thousand 
Pounds].  
In my opinion, the property represents a reasonable, good, or poor proposition for purchase 
at the agreed price, subject to the findings and recommendations contained within this report. 
Future maintenance and repair should be anticipated in accordance with the property's age, 
construction and level of ongoing maintenance. 
Reasonable with repair: This property is believed to be a reasonable proposition for 
purchase, given that you are prepared to cover the costs and accept the inconvenience of 
dealing with any repairs or improvement works reported. These defects are considered 
normal in properties of this age and construction. Provided that the works are carried out to a 
good standard, I cannot foresee any problems regarding a future resale of the property in 
normal market conditions.

entries.title: Construction
entries.rawBlock:
Type: The property is believed to be constructed using traditional masonry, timber frame, 
steel frame, system-built, or other construction. 
Roof type: The main roof is of pitched, flat, or mansard construction formed with 
traditional cut timber, prefabricated trussed rafters, or other structural members. 
Roof cover: The roof covering is formed in clay tiles, concrete tiles, natural slate, artificial 
slate, fibre cement slates, metal sheeting, mineral felt, rubber membrane, single-ply 
membrane, or other materials. 
External walls: The external walls are constructed of solid brick, cavity brick, stone, 
timber frame, rendered masonry, or other construction. 
Internal walls: Internal walls are formed in solid masonry, timber stud partitions, or a 
combination of both. 
Floors: Floors are of solid concrete, suspended timber, beam and block, or a combination 
of construction types. 
Windows: Windows are fitted with timber, PVCu, aluminium, or composite frames 
incorporating single, double, or triple glazing, where applicable. 
Construction has been identified from visible inspection only and has not been confirmed by 
opening concealed elements. 
If timber or steel frame is selected add this 
Modern Building Design: The building is believed to be of a modern design, framed 
internally with timber, steel or other materials, but most of the framework is concealed by on 
both sides with cladding. The durability of the structure is dependent upon the care taken 
during construction. For this reason, I cannot comment on the condition of the concealed 
structure, given the limited scope and technique of the inspection.  
Please, be aware that any alteration to this type of building will require a specialist advice 
from a qualified person. The exterior of the property must be adequately maintained to 
prevent water penetration. It is also important to reduce the risk of condensation that might 
encourage damage or weaken concealed components. When improving insulation, you should 
ensure that the material used is appropriate. You can only install insulation within the wall 
cavity with specialist advice.

entries.title: Outside the Property
entries.rawBlock:
Limitations 
My inspection of the exterior was carried out from ground level and other reasonably 
accessible positions.  
My inspection was restricted by the surrounding elements, including the layout of the area, 
and available vantage points from which I was able to view the property. 
Limitations: The inspection was limited by height, restricted access, nearby buildings, 
vegetation, weather conditions, roof configuration, or health and safety considerations. 
Restricted Access: There was no direct access to the rear of the building. For this reason, I 
cannot make any detailed comments regarding the condition of the uninspected walls, roof 
slopes, rainwater goods, etc. You should accept the risk that some defects may exist in these 
unseen areas. 
Roof coverings, chimney stacks and high-level elements were inspected using binoculars 
where appropriate. No parts of the building were opened up, dismantled or tested. 
Where elements were concealed or inaccessible, no comment can be made regarding their 
condition. 
Weather condition

detected when it is raining. 
Dry weather: It was more difficult to detect leakages to the chimney stacks, roof covering, 
and rainwater goods because it was not raining at the time of my inspection.

entries.title: Roof Coverings
entries.rawBlock:
Not Inspected: The roof covering(s) could not be inspected due to access restrictions and the 
height and configuration of the building. Consequently, I am unable to comment on their 
composition or condition. As the roof is exposed to the weather, it should be inspected 
regularly and maintained as necessary to identify and address any defects at an early stage. 
Description 
The pitched, mansard roof covering to the main building, extension, porch, or bay 
window, other is formed in original or replacement clay tiles, concrete tiles, natural 
slate, artificial slate, fibre cement slates, aluminium sheets, composite slate, asbestos 
sheet, other material. 
Condition: Where visible, the covering appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very 
poor condition. 
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified 
unless otherwise stated below. The roof structure appears to be adequately performing its 
functions. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age of the roof covering should be 
expected. 
Old roof covering: The roof covering over the building is old and may have reached or near 
the end of its useful life and will need to be stripped and renewed soon. If re-covered in 
heavier materials the timbers may need to be strengthened to comply with current Building 
Regulations. Further, although functioning satisfactorily, older roof coverings should be 
expected to require increased maintenance and eventual replacement as part of their normal 
service life. 
Repair soon: One or more tiles, slates, sheets roof covering are loose, missing, 
lifted, slipped, cracked, broken, distorted, other. This should be repaired soon. You 
should contact a qualified roofing contractor to carry out further investigation and 
replace or replaced damaged covering. 
Repair now: One or more tiles, slates, or roof covering sections are severely of 
significantly loose, missing, lifted, slipped, cracked, broken, distorted, other. This 
should be repaired now. The fixings on older roofs can weaken and result in more 
future maintenance. In some cases, it may be economical to replace the whole roof 
covering rather than continuing to repair. You should contact a qualified roofing 
contractor to carry out further investigation and recommend remedial work. 
Leaking: Because of the extent of observed roof covering defects, this is likely to 
cause damp penetration to the building below and is a safety hazard. This should be 
repaired urgently. You should contact a qualified roofing contractor to carry out 
further investigation and recommend remedial work now.

rubber membrane, single-ply membrane, GRP fibreglass, asphalt, lead, other material.

checks. Even though the general condition of the felt may appear satisfactory to type and age, 
repairs or replacement must be expected in the future. It is difficult to predict when this will 
be required as felt roofs can break down with little warning, even when visually appearing 
sound. 
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were 
identified unless otherwise stated below. The roof structure appears to be adequately 
performing its functions. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age of the roof 
covering should be expected.

entries.title: Rainwater Goods
entries.rawBlock:
Not Inspected: The rainwater goods could not be inspected due to access restrictions and the 
height and configuration of the building. Consequently, I am unable to comment on their 
composition or condition. As the roof is exposed to the weather, it should be inspected 
regularly and maintained as necessary to identify and address any defects at an early stage. 
Description 
The rainwater goods comprise PVC, cast iron, aluminium, steel, concrete, asbestos 
cement, other, gutters, downpipes, hoppers, and associated fittings. 
Condition: Where visible, the rainwater goods appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or 
very poor condition, consistent with their age and type. No parts of the rainwater installation 
were dismantled or tested. The adequacy of underground drainage has not been tested as part 
of this inspection. 
Rainwater discharging to ground: Some rainwater pipes have not been connected to gullies 
or extended sufficiently away from the building and allowed to drain directly to the ground. 
Rainwater can penetrate nearby structures and potentially cause internal dampness, timber 
rot, or erosion around the building. The discharge arrangement should be reviewed and 
improved where appropriate. 
Shared Rainwater Goods: The rainwater goods are believed to be shared with the adjoining 
property. Your legal adviser should confirm ownership, maintenance responsibilities and any 
rights or obligations affecting the shared installation. 
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified 
unless otherwise stated below. The rainwater goods appear to be adequately performing its 
functions. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age of the roof covering should be 
expected. 
If asbestos cement is selected, add the below 
The rainwater goods contain asbestos cement. Because of the possible asbestos content, you 
should get advice from a contractor experienced in this type of work or an asbestos specialist 
before the pipes or gutters are disturbed in any way. This includes activities such as cleaning 
out gutters, etc. 
Repairs 
Insufficient slope: The slope on the guttering is too shallow. This prevents the rainwater 
from draining properly and may result in future leaks. The gutters should be refitted with an 
adequate slope soon. You may have to replace parts of the system, and this can increase the 
amount of repair work. 
Damaged Sections: Sections of the gutters or downpipes are cracked, distorted, broken, 
split, missing, other. This should be repaired soon, now. Repairs or replacement should be 
undertaken to maintain the weather resistance of the building. 
Leakage: Staining to fittings and adjoining elements and localised dampness indicate 
previous or current leakage from the rainwater goods. This should be repaired soon, now. 
Repairs should be undertaken to prevent further deterioration of adjacent building elements. 
Blocked Gutters: Vegetation, moss, leaves, or other debris were observed within sections of 
the guttering. The gutters should be cleared as part of routine maintenance to maintain 
effective rainwater disposal. 
Blocked Gullies: One or more drainage gullies serving the rainwater system appear partially 
blocked or fully blocked. Blocked gullies may result in localised flooding and water 
penetration to adjacent building elements. The gullies should be cleared and maintained 
regularly. 
Defective Connections: One or more gutter joints or downpipe connections are loose, 
missing, leaking, displaced, defective, other. This should be repaired soon, now. Repairs 
should be undertaken to maintain the effectiveness of the rainwater system. 
Corrosion: Sections of the rainwater goods exhibit light, moderate, or significant corrosion. 
Corroded sections should be repaired or replaced where necessary to maintain satisfactory 
performance. This should be repaired promptly if the damage is significant.  
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building - One or more defects affecting the rainwater 
gutters, downpipes, associated fittings and drainage arrangements were noted. 
General Maintenance: Rainwater goods should be inspected and cleared at regular intervals, 
particularly during the autumn and following severe weather. Routine maintenance will assist 
in preventing blockages, overflow, water penetration and premature deterioration. 
If the Property is a Flat, add this  
You should ask the management company whether any repairs to the rainwater goods have 
been carried out previously or are currently proposed. Your legal adviser should confirm 
responsibility for repairs to the rainwater goods with the management company and ensure 
that an adequate sinking or reserve fund is in place to meet the cost of future repairs or 
replacement, should the need arise. This may help reduce the risk of unexpected repair costs 
or increases in the service charge. 
Condition rating 123

entries.title: Main Walls
entries.rawBlock:
The external walls have been inspected visually and by touch from the outside and internally 
where exposed. No opening up or destructive investigation has been undertaken. The 
composition of the wall material cannot be fully confirmed without causing damage to the 
walls. 
Description 
The external walls of the main building, extension(s), other, are constructed of 000 mm 
solid brick, cavity brick, timber frame, rendered masonry, blockwork, other 
construction types. 
Cladding: Cladding: The external wall finish or cladding comprise facing brickwork, 
render, pebble dash, stone, timber cladding, weatherboarding, fibre cement boards, 
plastic boards, compressed flat panels, composite panels, glass, tile hanging, terracotta 
tiles, other finishes. 
Condition: Where visible, the walls appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor 
condition, consistent with their age and type of construction. 
No repair required: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified 
unless otherwise stated below. The external walls appear to be adequately performing its 
functions. Routine maintenance appropriate to the age of the roof covering should be 
expected. 
Cavity Wall Insulation: There is evidence that cavity wall insulation has been installed. 
Your legal adviser should verify the type of insulation used, the date of installation, and 
whether any guarantees or warranties are available. 
If it is confirmed that foam cavity wall insulation has been installed, please note that this type 
of insulation has been associated with problems in some properties. These may include 
deterioration of the insulation over time, allowing moisture to bridge the cavity and resulting 
in internal dampness, or contributing to the accelerated corrosion of wall ties where 
conditions are conducive. The availability of any guarantees or warranties should also be 
confirmed. 
Thin wall: The external wall to the front, rear, side wall of the main building, extension is 
not thick enough and vulnerable to damp problems and heat loss. This sub-standard 
construction should be improved soon. In some cases, rebuilding the wall to modern 
standards may be the only economic option. 
Damp-proof course: The walls have a barrier against dampness rising from the ground 
(called a damp-proof course or DPC is visible, partially visible, or not visible, one would 
normally be expected for a property of this age and type.  The DPC is assumed to consist of 
plastic, felt, slates, engineering bricks, other. The adequacy of concealed damp-proof 
courses cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
DPC Treatment noted: I noted evidence of damp proof course treatment, 
ventilation apparatus, ventilation holes, other in the property. You should ask your 
legal adviser to check whether there has been a dampness problem before and if a 
valid guarantee or warranty covers this work.   
If not, you should ask an appropriately qualified person to inspect the property, assess 
its condition and identify what repairs are required. Once the repairs have been 
completed, this person should issue a certificate of 'structural worthiness'. You 
should ask your insurance company if this problem would affect your ability to get 
insurance cover for this property. 
Add text to: Section I2 - Guarantees - You should ask your legal adviser to confirm 
whether the damp proof course treatment is covered by a guarantee or warranty and 
advice on the implications. 
Damp and moisture readings 
Random moisture readings were taken to accessible internal wall surfaces using a hand-held 
electronic moisture meter. 
No damp found: No readings were obtained that suggest abnormal moisture levels at 
the time of inspection. 
Damp found: Elevated moisture readings were recorded to sections of the internal 
wall surfaces the include enter location(s). 
Penetrating damp: This may have been affected by penetrating damp probably 
caused by overflowing gutter, roof leak, leaking downpipe, bridged DPC, blocked 
gully, other. When the problem has been resolved, the wall may need to be repaired. 
Repair options: The source of the moisture should be identified and remedied as a 
priority. This may involve repairs to the gutters, roof covering, downpipes, damp-
proof course, gullies, drainage, other, as appropriate. Once the source of moisture 
has been eliminated and the affected walls have been allowed sufficient time to dry 
naturally, any damaged plaster, decorations or other finishes should be repaired or 
replaced as necessary. The affected area should then be monitored to ensure that the 
dampness does not recur. 
Investigate cause: The source of moisture cannot be confirmed during a visual 
inspection. You should instruct a suitably qualified contractor to investigate the cause 
of the dampness and carry out any necessary repairs to prevent further moisture 
penetration. Following completion of the repairs, the affected walls should be allowed 
to dry before any replastering, redecoration or replacement of finishes is undertaken. 
Premature redecoration may result in the recurrence of staining or damage if residual 
moisture remains within the wall. 
Rising damp: This may have been affected by rising damp probably caused by 
damaged DPC, old and brittle DPC, bridged DPC, defective drainage, other. 
When the problem has been resolved, the wall may need to be repaired. 
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building - Elevated moisture readings were 
recorded to sections of the internal wall surfaces the include enter location(s). 
Add text to: Section J3 - Risk to people - Elevated moisture readings were recorded 
to sections of the internal wall surfaces the include enter location(s). 
Drainage guttering: Because the external ground levels are high in relation to the building, 
the damp-proof course (DPC) may be bridged in places, allowing moisture to penetrate the 
walls. External ground levels should be reduced where practicable to maintain an appropriate 
clearance below the damp-proof course. Where this is not feasible, suitable drainage 
measures, such as a French drain or gravel-filled drainage channel, may be appropriate to 
improve surface water drainage and reduce the risk of moisture penetration. A suitably 
qualified contractor should advise on the most appropriate remedial solution. 
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building - The external ground levels are high in relation 
to the building, the damp-proof course (DPC) may be bridged in places, allowing moisture to 
penetrate the walls. 
Removed wall: An external wall to the lounge, kitchen, bedroom, other appears to have 
been removed as part of previous alterations. This work should have been carried out with 
Building Regulations approval and should have included adequate structural support for the 
remaining wall above the openings. Due to the internal floor and ceiling finishes, I was 
unable to confirm whether suitable structural support has been provided. I strongly 
recommend that your legal adviser obtains confirmation that the necessary Building 
Regulations approval was obtained for these alterations. If the required approval cannot be 
confirmed, or the work was not properly supervised, there is a risk that additional structural 
support may be required. This could result in further investigation, remedial works, additional 
costs, and disruption. 
Defect noted: I noted cracking, distortions, other in the surrounding wall surfaces. 
However, due to the concealed nature of the structure behind the wall and the floor 
and ceiling finishes, I was unable to confirm whether adequate structural support has 
been provided. You should instruct a suitably qualified structural engineer to carry out 
further investigation and advise on the adequacy of the structural alterations and any 
remedial works that may be required. 
Extensions and alterations: Evidence was noted that external alterations have been carried 
out to the property. These include wall removal, new openings, replacement lintels, 
structural alterations, extension works, or other alterations. 
Your legal adviser should confirm that all appropriate statutory approvals and completion 
certificates have been obtained where required. 
Add text to: Section I1 - Regulations -Evidence was noted that external alterations have 
been carried out to the property. These include wall removal, new openings, replacement 
lintels, structural alterations, extension works, or other alterations. 
Structural Movement: None: Although I did not observe any evidence of significant 
structural movement during my inspection, I cannot be categorical that none has occurred, as 
all buildings are subject to some degree of movement, such as normal settlement and seasonal 
thermal or moisture-related movement. It is also possible that evidence of movement, 
including cracks, may be concealed by floor coverings, decorations, fitted furniture or other 
obstructions.  
Normal: I noted no evidence of any significant recent or progressive structural 
movement within the property. However, there are signs that the property has 
experienced some historic movement, as evidenced by cracking to external and 
internal wall surfaces, at junctions and around openings. As far as could be observed, 
these cracks appear longstanding in nature, and there is no evidence to suggest 
significant ongoing movement. No significant repairs are considered necessary at this 
time, although localised repairs and redecoration may be required as part of routine 
maintenance. 
Recent: The front, side, rear walls of the main building, back addition, extension, 
bay window, porch, other have been damaged by movement cracks potentially 
arising from settlement, subsidence, nearby vegetation, point loading, wall tie 
damage, other and this is structurally serious. Movement within the property is 
considered serious and could worsen over time. Parts of the property could become 
unstable. You should instruct an appropriately qualified structural engineer to 
investigate the problem and recommend an appropriate scheme of repair. To carry out 
a proper investigation, it is likely that parts of the property will need to be opened or 
disturbed, and this should be discussed with the building owner. Evidence of previous 
structural movement, even where satisfactorily resolved, may affect the property's 
future mortgageability and saleability. 
Add text to: Section I2 - Guarantees - The front, side, rear walls of the main 
building, back addition, extension, bay window, porch, other have been damaged by 
movement cracks potentially arising from settlement, subsidence, nearby vegetation, 
point loading, wall tie damage, other and this is structurally serious.   
Recurring:  The outside wall(s) to the main building, back addition, extension, bay 
window, porch, other have been repaired, indicating that the building has been 
affected by previous movement. However, recent cracking suggests that movement 
may have recurred. This may indicate that the previous repairs have not been fully 
effective. You should ask your legal adviser to establish whether any guarantees, 
warranties or insurance-backed schemes are available in relation to these repairs. If 
satisfactory information cannot be obtained, you should instruct an appropriately 
qualified structural engineer to investigate the cause and extent of the movement and 
recommend an appropriate scheme of repair. Evidence of previous structural 
movement, even where satisfactorily resolved, may affect the property's future 
mortgageability and saleability. 
Add text to: Section I2 - Guarantees - Recent cracking suggests that movement may 
have recurred. This may indicate that the previous repairs have not been fully 
effective. You should ask your legal adviser to establish whether any guarantees, 
warranties or insurance-backed schemes are available in relation to these repairs.  
Trees: There are trees located close to the property. I noted no obvious signs to suggest that 
they have caused significant damage to the property. However, it would be prudent to 
implement a programme of management to control their future growth. Trees can affect 
building foundations and below-ground services, particularly where shrinkable subsoils are 
present. 
Defects noted: There are trees located close to the property, and I noted defects that 
may be associated with their influence, including cracking, distortion, heave, other 
observed defects. Although the cause cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection, 
further investigation by a suitably qualified structural engineer and, where 
appropriate, an arboriculturist is recommended to establish whether the trees are 
contributing to the observed defects and to advise on any necessary remedial works. 
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building - There are trees located close to the 
property, and I noted defects that may be associated with their influence. 
Spalled Brickwork: A few bricks exhibit minor, moderate, or significant deterioration 
(this is called spalling). Damaged bricks should be replaced where deterioration is sufficient 
to affect the weather resistance of the wall. 
Causing damp: This is allowing damp to get into the building. These should be 
repaired now. 
Repair pointing: The mortar between the bricks (known as the pointing) to parts of the 
building is eroded, loose, missing, damaged, other. The defective pointing should be 
renewed using a mortar appropriate to the age, type and construction of the building. This 
may comprise lime-based mortar or Portland cement mortar, as appropriate. Weathered or 
defective pointing should be renewed as part of routine maintenance to help reduce water 
penetration and minimise further deterioration. 
Causing damp: This is allowing damp to get into the building. These should be 
repaired now. 
Repair render: Parts of the render coating to the building is eroded, loose, missing, 
damaged, other. The defective pointing should be renewed using a mortar appropriate to the 
age, type and construction of the building. This may comprise lime-based mortar or Portland 
cement mortar, as appropriate. Weathered or defective pointing should be renewed as part of 
routine maintenance to help reduce water penetration and minimise further deterioration. 
Hazard: Rendering pieces are likely to fall and cause harm to people that may be 
nearby. This is a hazard and this repair should be carried out urgently. 
Causing damp: This is allowing damp to get into the building. These should be 
repaired now. 
Add text to: Section J3 - Risk to people - Parts of the render coating to the building is 
eroded, loose, missing, damaged, other.  
Wall Ties: Parts of the walls to the side of the property show evidence of previous cavity 
wall tie repairs. No further repairs appear necessary based on my visual inspection, and the 
property should be maintained in the normal way. You should ask your legal adviser to 
confirm whether any guarantees, warranties or completion certificates are available for these 
works. If satisfactory documentation is not available, you should instruct a suitably qualified 
specialist to inspect the walls and confirm that the repairs remain satisfactory. 
Wall Tie Defect: There are signs that may be consistent with defective cavity wall 
ties. Defective wall ties can affect the stability of cavity walls if left untreated. You 
should instruct a suitably qualified specialist to carry out a detailed inspection, 
confirm the condition of the wall ties and recommend any necessary remedial works. 
Your legal adviser should also establish whether any guarantees or warranties are 
available in relation to previous repairs, if applicable. 
Repair lintels soon: The small beam that spans across the top of the door opening including 
brick arch (called a lintel) in the front, side, rear, other wall of the main building, back 
addition, extension, bay window, other is damaged, cracked, distorted. This should be 
repaired soon.  
To repair the lintel properly, it may have to be replaced completely. Cracked or deteriorated 
lintels should be further investigated and repaired where necessary. 
Repair lintels now: The small beam that spans across the top of the window or door opening 
including brick arch (called a lintel) in the front, side, rear, other wall of the main building, 
back addition, extension, bay window, other is damaged, cracked, distorted. The defect is 
causing the window frame to distort. A new lintel or arch may be needed, and you may have 
to organise associated repairs. This can increase the amount of repair work required. 
Add text to: Section J1 - Risk to Building - The small beam that spans across the top of the 
window or door opening including brick arch (called a lintel) in the front, side, rear, other

Repair windowsill soon: The small beam that spans across the bottom of the window

To repair the windowsill properly, it may have to be replaced completely. Cracked or

Repair windowsill now: The small beam that spans across the bottom of the window

entries.title: Windows
entries.rawBlock:
Not every part of the windows was inspected in detail. The inspection was limited to those 
parts that were readily accessible without causing damage or moving furnishings. Only a 
representative sample of accessible windows was opened and closed during the inspection. 
Windows obscured by curtains, blinds, shutters, furniture, stored items, or fitted security 
devices could not be fully inspected. Double-glazed units cannot be tested for thermal 
performance during a visual inspection. 
Description 
The windows are formed predominantly of replacement, original, old, PVCu, timber, old 
style timber sash, aluminium, composite, modern PVC sash, modern timber sash, other 
framed units. 
Glazing: The glazing comprises single glazing, double glazing, triple glazing, decorative 
glazing, other glazing types. 
Condition: Where visible and operated during the inspection, the windows appear in good, 
reasonable, fair, poor, very poor condition, consistent with their age and type. 
No defects noted: No significant defects requiring immediate attention were 
identified unless otherwise stated below. Routine maintenance appropriate to the 
frame material should be expected. 
If very poor is selected, add this  
Windows that are in poor condition or in disrepair will require comprehensive repair. 
In some cases, it may be more economical to replace the windows entirely. This work 
should be done under an appropriate FENSA, CERTASS, or Building Regulation 
approval scheme where applicable. Applicable guarantees or warranties should be 
obtained. 
No BS EN noted: No visible British Standard, BS EN, or other permanent safety 
markings were identified to the accessible glazing. The absence of visible markings 
does not necessarily indicate that safety glazing has not been installed. Where 
confirmation is required, your legal adviser should verify any available certification 
relating to replacement windows. 
BS EN noted: Visible British Standard, BS EN, or other permanent safety markings 
were identified to the accessible glazing. The presence of visible markings indicate 
that safety glazing has been installed. Where confirmation is required, your legal 
adviser should verify any available certification relating to replacement windows. 
If replacement window is selected, add this  
The windows appear to have been fully replaced or partially replaced. Where 
replacement windows have been installed, your legal adviser should confirm that the 
installation was carried out under an appropriate FENSA, CERTASS, or Building 
Regulation approval scheme where applicable. Any available guarantees or warranties 
should also be obtained. 
If old style timber sash is selected, add this  
Double-hung sash windows are expensive to maintain and tend to be ill-fitting and 
allow heat loss. From time to time, it is important to employ a joiner to inspect the 
sash windows, check the cording and to ease them before redecoration. This is best 
down in conjunction with the redecoration cycle. 
Add text to: Section J2 Guarantees - You should ask your legal adviser to confirm 
whether the PVC glazed sections to the windows were installed by a contractor 
registered with FENSA. Enquiries should also be made regarding any guarantees or 
warranties for the double glazing. 
Glazing seals: The external sealant around the window frames appears in good, reasonable, 
fair, poor, or very poor condition. Defective sealant should be renewed to reduce the risk of 
water penetration. 
Sill projection: Externally, the windowsills beyond the face of the walls appear to project 
adequately beyond the face of the walls. The junctions between the window frames and the 
surrounding wall openings appear to be properly, fairly, poorly sealed. These seals should 
be inspected regularly for cracking and repaired as necessary to prevent water ingress. 
Sill defect: The windowsill(s) projection beyond the face of the wall(s) does not 
appear to be adequate, properly installed or drained, cracked or have other defects. 
This is allowing water ingress to adjoining walls and may be causing dampness. You 
should promptly arrange for further investigation and repair by a qualified 
professional to prevent further damages.  
Repair windows: The window(s) in the lounge, bedroom, kitchen, other, have damaged 
lock(s), missing lock(s), are difficult to open, are badly worn, are rotten, have broken 
panes, have failed glazing, are in disrepair, severely damaged, present a safety hazard, 
other. These should be repaired without delay, as the security of the property may be 
compromised. However, severely or significantly damaged window(s) should be repaired 
immediately.  
Add text to: Section J3 Risk to people - One or more windows have been affected by single

and cannot provide absolute assurance that concealed surfaces or structural elements are free 
from moisture-related defects. Weather conditions, temperature and humidity can all 
influence moisture levels and the observations made during an inspection. Where my findings 
are inconclusive regarding the extent or cause of dampness, I recommend that you arrange a 
further investigation by a suitably qualified independent specialist. The inspection should be 
carried out in accordance with the Joint Position Statement (JPS) 2022, Investigation of 
Moisture and its Effects on Traditional Buildings, and should be undertaken independently of 
any contractor providing quotations for remedial work. 
The inspection was visual and non-invasive. Floor coverings were not lifted, furniture and 
stored items were not moved, and no opening up or destructive investigation was undertaken. 
Comments relate only to the condition observed at the time of the inspection. 
The inspection of the internal accommodation was limited by fitted floor coverings, 
furniture, stored items, fixed fittings, restricted access, locked rooms, limited roof 
access, limited lighting, or health and safety considerations. 
Roof Spaces: Where roof space access was available, only those areas that could be 
inspected safely from the access hatch and boarded areas were examined. Insulation, stored 
items, roof timbers and restricted headroom may have limited the inspection. Areas that were 
inaccessible have not been inspected.

entries.title: Roof Structure
entries.rawBlock:
Description 
The roof structure was inspected from the roof access hatch where available and from those 
areas that were safely accessible at the time of the inspection. 
The roof structure is formed in traditional cut timber, prefabricated trussed rafters, steel, 
or a combination of construction types. 
Where visible, the roof structure appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor 
condition, consistent with its age and construction. 
No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless otherwise stated 
below. 
Roof Structure 
The roof structure is formed in traditional cut timber, prefabricated trussed rafters, 
engineered timber, or a combination of structural members. 
Where visible, the roof timbers appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor 
condition. 
No significant distortion was observed unless otherwise stated. 
Roof Underlay 
The underside of the roof covering incorporates traditional bituminous felt, breathable 
membrane, sarking boards, or no underlay, where visible. 
Where visible, the underlay appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
The absence of underlay may be consistent with the age and type of construction and does not 
necessarily indicate a defect. 
Roof Ventilation 
The roof space appears to have adequate, limited, or restricted ventilation. 
Adequate roof space ventilation assists in reducing the risk of condensation and timber decay. 
Where ventilation is limited, improvements should be considered when future roofing works 
are undertaken. 
Thermal Insulation 
The roof space insulation appears adequate, limited, or insufficient based upon the visible 
areas only. 
The thickness and continuity of insulation cannot be confirmed without disturbing the 
insulation. 
Reference should also be made to the Energy Performance Certificate where available. 
Water Storage Tanks 
The roof space contains plastic, galvanised steel, or other cold water storage tanks. 
Where visible, the tank appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
No evidence of leakage was observed at the time of inspection unless otherwise stated. 
Water Tank Insulation 
The water tank and associated pipework appear adequately insulated, partially insulated, 
or uninsulated. 
Improving insulation may reduce the risk of freezing and heat loss. 
Disused Water Tank 
A plastic, galvanised steel, or other disused water storage tank remains within the roof 
space. 
Removal may be considered during future maintenance where it is no longer required. 
Roof Timbers 
Where visible, the roof timbers appear dry, sound, and adequately supported. 
or 
Localised distortion, splitting, cracking, notching, or alterations were observed. 
Repairs or further investigation should be undertaken where structural adequacy is uncertain. 
Timber Decay 
No visible evidence of active timber decay was observed to the accessible roof timbers. 
or 
Evidence of wet rot, dry rot, or fungal decay was observed. 
The source of moisture should be identified and rectified before repairs are undertaken. 
Wood-Boring Insects 
No visible evidence of active wood-boring insect infestation was observed to the accessible 
roof timbers. 
Historic flight holes may be present and are not necessarily indicative of active infestation. 
or 
Evidence of active or historic wood-boring insect activity was observed. 
Further inspection by an appropriately qualified timber specialist is recommended where 
activity appears active or widespread. 
Roof Movement 
No evidence of significant movement or distortion was observed to the roof structure. 
or 
Evidence of deflection, sagging, spread, or distortion was observed. 
Further investigation by an appropriately qualified structural engineer or roofing contractor is 
recommended where movement appears significant. 
Roof Loading 
There is no visible evidence that the roof covering is imposing excessive loading upon the 
roof structure. 
or 
The roof covering appears heavier than would normally be expected for the original roof 
structure. 
Further assessment should be undertaken where structural adequacy is uncertain. 
Structural Alterations 
Evidence of structural alterations to the roof space was observed, including loft conversion, 
altered roof members, removed struts, trimmed rafters, replacement supports, or other 
alterations. 
The adequacy of structural support cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Your legal adviser should confirm that appropriate statutory approvals and completion 
certificates were obtained where applicable. 
Chimney Breast Alterations 
Evidence was observed that a chimney breast has been removed, partially removed, or 
altered within the roof space. 
The adequacy of structural support cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Your legal adviser should confirm that appropriate approvals were obtained where applicable. 
Where structural adequacy is uncertain, further investigation by an appropriately qualified 
structural engineer is recommended. 
Party Wall 
The party wall appears continuous within the roof space where visible. 
or 
Gaps or defects were observed within the party wall construction. 
Repairs should be undertaken to maintain fire separation and reduce the risk of fire spread 
between adjoining properties. 
Evidence of Water Penetration 
No visible evidence of active water penetration was observed to the accessible roof structure 
at the time of inspection. 
or 
Water staining or dampness was observed to roof timbers, underlay or adjacent structural 
elements. 
The source should be identified and repaired to prevent further deterioration. 
General Maintenance 
Roof spaces should remain adequately ventilated and free from unnecessary stored items that 
may restrict inspection or ventilation. 
Roof timbers should be inspected whenever significant roofing works are undertaken. 
Prompt attention to water penetration will reduce the risk of timber decay and associated 
structural deterioration.

entries.title: Ceilings
entries.rawBlock:
Description 
The ceilings have been inspected from within the rooms only. No opening up or destructive 
investigation has been undertaken. 
The ceilings are formed in plaster, plasterboard, lath and plaster, or a combination of 
ceiling types. 
The ceiling finish comprises painted, textured coating, papered, timber clad, tiled, or a 
combination of finishes. 
Where visible, the ceilings appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition, 
consistent with their age and construction. 
No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless otherwise stated 
below. 
Inspection Limitations 
The inspection was limited by floor coverings above, fixed light fittings, fitted furniture, 
stored items, high ceilings, or restricted access. 
The ceiling construction and concealed structural members cannot be confirmed without 
opening up the structure. 
Ceiling Construction 
The ceilings are formed in plasterboard, lath and plaster, solid plaster, or a combination 
of construction types. 
Where visible, they appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
Ceiling Finish 
The ceiling finish comprises paint, textured coating, wallpaper, timber cladding, 
decorative panels, or a combination of finishes. 
Where visible, the finish appears in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
Routine redecoration appropriate to the age and condition of the property should be expected. 
Cracking 
Minor shrinkage cracking was observed to the ceiling finish. 
Such cracking is common in properties of this age and type and is not generally considered 
structurally significant. 
The cracks may be filled and redecorated during routine maintenance. 
or 
Significant cracking was observed to the ceiling. 
Further investigation is recommended where cracking appears progressive or is associated 
with distortion. 
Unevenness 
Minor undulations or unevenness were noted to the ceiling surfaces. 
These are not uncommon in properties of this age and do not necessarily indicate structural 
movement. 
or 
Noticeable deflection or distortion was observed. 
Further investigation should be undertaken where structural movement is suspected. 
Water Staining 
No visible evidence of water staining was observed. 
or 
Water staining or localised dampness was noted to the ceiling. 
The source of moisture should be identified and repaired before redecoration. 
Water Damage 
Localised damage consistent with previous water penetration was observed. 
Although the affected area appears dry at the time of inspection, repairs and redecoration 
should be undertaken as required. 
Textured Coatings 
The ceilings are finished with textured coating. 
Older textured coatings may contain asbestos fibres. 
Where future disturbance or removal is proposed, specialist advice should be obtained before 
work is undertaken. 
Polystyrene Ceiling Tiles 
The ceilings incorporate polystyrene ceiling tiles. 
These should be regarded as a potential fire hazard, and replacement should be considered 
during future refurbishment. 
Heavy Decorative Finishes 
The ceilings are covered with lining paper, decorative coverings, or other applied finishes. 
These finishes may conceal minor defects and may require local repairs when removed 
during future redecoration. 
Asbestos 
Some ceiling materials may contain asbestos depending upon their age and construction. 
Where materials remain in good condition and are left undisturbed, they do not normally 
present a significant health risk. 
Specialist advice should be obtained before any disturbance, alteration or removal. 
Ceiling Junctions 
Minor cracking was noted at the junction between ceilings and walls. 
This is commonly associated with normal thermal movement and shrinkage. 
Repairs may be undertaken during routine redecoration. 
General Maintenance 
Ceilings should be inspected periodically for signs of cracking, distortion or water 
penetration. 
Prompt repair of roof leaks, plumbing defects and condensation problems will reduce the 
likelihood of damage to internal ceiling finishes. 
Routine redecoration should be expected throughout the normal life of the property.

entries.title: Walls and Partitions
entries.rawBlock:
Description 
The internal walls and partitions have been inspected from within the rooms only. No 
opening up or destructive investigation has been undertaken. 
The walls are formed in solid masonry, timber stud partitions, plasterboard partitions, or 
a combination of construction types. 
The wall finishes comprise paint, plaster, wallpaper, ceramic tiling, timber panelling, or a 
combination of finishes. 
Where visible, the walls and partitions appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor 
condition, consistent with their age and construction. 
No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless otherwise stated 
below. 
Inspection Limitations 
The inspection was limited by fixed furniture, kitchen units, bathroom fittings, wall 
coverings, stored items, large appliances, or restricted access. 
The condition of concealed wall construction, hidden lintels and structural supports cannot be 
confirmed without opening up the structure. 
Areas concealed by fitted cupboards, tiled finishes or decorative wall coverings could not be 
fully inspected. 
Wall Construction 
The internal walls are formed in solid masonry, timber stud partitions, plasterboard 
partitions, or a combination of construction types. 
Where visible, they appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
Wall Finishes 
The wall finishes comprise paint, plaster, wallpaper, ceramic tiling, decorative panelling, 
or a combination of finishes. 
Where visible, the finishes appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
Routine redecoration appropriate to the age and condition of the property should be expected. 
Cracking 
Minor shrinkage cracking was observed to internal wall finishes. 
Such cracking is common in properties of this age and type and is not generally considered 
structurally significant. 
The affected areas may be filled and redecorated during routine maintenance. 
or 
Noticeable cracking was observed to internal wall surfaces. 
Further investigation is recommended where cracking appears progressive, is associated with 
distortion, or is indicative of structural movement. 
Structural Movement 
No evidence of significant structural movement was observed to the accessible internal wall 
surfaces. 
or 
Evidence of historic, localised, or progressive movement was observed. 
Where movement appears progressive or structurally significant, further investigation by an 
appropriately qualified structural engineer is recommended before legal commitment. 
Dampness 
Random moisture readings were taken to accessible wall surfaces using a hand-held 
electronic moisture meter. 
No elevated moisture readings were recorded at the time of inspection. 
or 
Elevated moisture readings were recorded to sections of the wall surfaces. 
The source of moisture cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Further investigation should be undertaken where moisture levels remain elevated or visible 
dampness is present. 
Condensation 
Evidence of condensation and localised mould growth was observed to external walls, 
window reveals, bedrooms, bathrooms, kitchens, or other areas. 
Condensation is commonly associated with occupancy patterns, heating, insulation and 
ventilation. 
Maintaining a suitable balance between heating and ventilation should assist in reducing 
condensation. 
Penetrating Damp 
Localised dampness consistent with penetrating moisture was observed. 
The source should be identified and repaired before internal redecoration is undertaken. 
Internal Alterations 
Evidence was observed that an internal wall has been removed, partially removed, altered, 
or that a new opening has been formed. 
No evidence of structural concerns was observed during the inspection. 
or 
Cracking or distortion was noted adjacent to the alteration. 
The adequacy of concealed structural support cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Your legal adviser should confirm that appropriate Building Regulation approval and 
completion certification were obtained where applicable. 
Tiled Wall Areas 
Parts of the wall surfaces are concealed behind ceramic tiling, stone finishes, decorative 
panelling, or fixed fittings. 
The concealed condition of these wall surfaces cannot be confirmed. 
Hollow Plaster 
Localised hollow-sounding plaster was identified. 
This commonly indicates a loss of adhesion between the plaster and the background surface. 
Repairs may be required where affected areas become loose or detached. 
Sealants 
The sealant at the junction between wall finishes and sanitary fittings appears in good, 
reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
Defective sealant should be renewed to reduce the risk of water penetration behind the 
fittings. 
General Maintenance 
Internal walls should be inspected periodically for signs of cracking, dampness or movement. 
Minor cracking and decorative defects should be repaired during routine maintenance. 
Maintaining adequate heating and ventilation will assist in reducing the risk of condensation 
and mould growth.

entries.title: Floors
entries.rawBlock:

were not lifted, and no opening up or destructive investigation was undertaken. 
The floors are formed in solid concrete, suspended timber, beam and block, or a 
combination of construction types.

Where visible, the floors appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition,

No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless otherwise stated 
below. 
Inspection Limitations 
The inspection was limited by fitted floor coverings, furniture, stored items, fixed kitchen 
units, bathroom fittings, or restricted access. 
The condition of concealed floor timbers, floor voids, joists, sleeper walls and foundations 
cannot be confirmed without lifting floor finishes or opening up the structure. 
Only the visible performance of the floors was assessed during normal use. 
Floor Construction 
The floors are of solid concrete, suspended timber, beam and block, or a combination of 
construction types. 
No opening up was undertaken to confirm the exact construction. 
Floor Finishes 
The floor finishes comprise carpet, laminate flooring, timber flooring, vinyl, ceramic tiles, 
stone, or a combination of finishes. 
Where visible, the finishes appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
Routine maintenance and replacement due to normal wear should be expected throughout the 
life of the property. 
General Performance 
The floors felt firm, reasonably firm, or slightly uneven when walked upon. 
No significant movement was observed unless otherwise stated. 
Minor creaking to suspended timber floors is common in properties of this age and type and 
does not necessarily indicate a structural defect. 
Uneven Floors 
Minor unevenness was noted to sections of the floor. 
This is not uncommon in properties of this age and does not necessarily indicate structural 
movement. 
or 
Noticeable unevenness or deflection was observed. 
Further investigation is recommended where the extent or cause cannot be determined during 
a visual inspection. 
Creaking Floors 
Localised creaking was noted to the suspended timber floors.

joists. 
Repairs may be undertaken as part of routine maintenance where considered necessary. 
Floor Tiles 
The floor tiles appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
No significant defects were observed unless otherwise stated. 
or 
Localised cracked, loose, or damaged floor tiles were observed. 
Repairs should be undertaken to maintain the floor finish and reduce the risk of further 
deterioration. 
Dampness 
No visible evidence of dampness was observed to the accessible floor surfaces. 
or 
Evidence of dampness was observed to the floor surfaces. 
The source of moisture cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Further investigation should be undertaken where dampness persists. 
Timber Decay 
No visible evidence of timber decay was observed to the accessible floor timbers. 
or 
Evidence of wet rot, dry rot, or timber deterioration was observed. 
The source of moisture should be identified and repaired before remedial timber repairs are 
undertaken. 
Wood-Boring Insects 
No visible evidence of active wood-boring insect infestation was observed to the accessible 
timber floors. 
Historic flight holes may be present and are not necessarily indicative of active infestation. 
or 
Evidence of active or historic wood-boring insect activity was observed. 
Further inspection by an appropriately qualified timber specialist is recommended where 
activity appears active or widespread. 
Underfloor Ventilation 
Where applicable, the suspended timber floor is provided with adequate, limited, or 
restricted underfloor ventilation. 
Adequate ventilation is important in reducing the risk of condensation and timber decay. 
Where ventilation appears restricted, improvements should be considered during future 
maintenance works. 
Structural Movement 
No evidence of significant structural movement was observed affecting the floor structure. 
or 
Evidence of deflection, distortion, or movement was observed. 
Further investigation by an appropriately qualified structural engineer is recommended where 
structural movement appears significant. 
Concealed Defects 
Because floor coverings were not lifted, concealed defects may exist that could not 
reasonably be identified during a visual inspection. 
No comment can therefore be made regarding the condition of concealed floor timbers or 
supporting construction. 
General Maintenance 
Floors should be inspected periodically for signs of movement, dampness or deterioration. 
Prompt repair of plumbing leaks, water penetration and defective ventilation will reduce the 
risk of damage to concealed floor timbers. 
Floor finishes should be repaired or replaced as part of normal property maintenance when 
they reach the end of their service life.

entries.title: Fireplaces, Chimney Breasts and Flues
entries.rawBlock:
Description 
This section relates to visible fireplaces, chimney breasts and associated flues within the 
property. 
The inspection was limited to a visual assessment only. Fireplaces, flues and appliances were 
not tested, dismantled or operated unless otherwise stated. 
Where visible, the fireplaces and chimney breasts appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or 
very poor condition, consistent with their age and construction. 
No significant defects requiring immediate attention were identified unless otherwise stated 
below. 
Inspection Limitations 
The inspection was limited by fixed fittings, decorative finishes, stored items, furniture, 
restricted access, or blocked fireplaces. 
The internal condition of chimney flues, liners and concealed structural elements cannot be 
confirmed during a visual inspection. 
No smoke testing, CCTV survey or opening up was undertaken. 
Fireplace Construction 
The property incorporates open fireplaces, gas fires, electric fires, solid fuel stoves, wood-
burning stoves, multi-fuel stoves, or decorative fireplaces. 
Where visible, these appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
Open Fireplaces 
The property incorporates open fireplaces. 
No functional testing has been undertaken. 
If the fireplace is to be used, it should be inspected and tested by an appropriately qualified 
chimney specialist before use. 
Gas Fires 
The property incorporates gas fires. 
Gas appliances were not tested during the inspection. 
Their condition, safety and serviceability should be confirmed by a Gas Safe registered 
engineer before legal commitment. 
Wood-Burning or Multi-Fuel Stoves 
The property incorporates a wood-burning stove or multi-fuel stove. 
The appliance was not tested. 
The installation, flue and associated components should be inspected and serviced in 
accordance with the manufacturer's recommendations. 
Electric Fires 
The property incorporates electric fires. 
No operational testing was undertaken. 
Their serviceability cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Chimney Breasts 
The chimney breasts appear original, altered, partially removed, or removed. 
Where visible, they appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition. 
No significant defects were observed unless otherwise stated. 
Removed Chimney Breasts 
Evidence was observed that a chimney breast has been partially removed or removed. 
The adequacy of concealed structural support cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Your legal adviser should confirm that appropriate Building Regulation approval and 
completion certification were obtained where applicable. 
Where structural adequacy is uncertain, further investigation by an appropriately qualified 
structural engineer is recommended. 
Fireplace Openings 
The fireplace opening appears original, altered, blocked, or sealed.

where appropriate. 
Chimney Flues 
The chimney flues were not inspected internally.

inspection. 
If the flues are to be used, they should be inspected and tested by an appropriately qualified 
chimney specialist before use. 
Flue Liners 
The presence or condition of flue liners cannot be confirmed during a visual inspection. 
Where replacement heating appliances have been installed, appropriate certification should 
be obtained where available. 
Ventilation 
Combustion appliances should be provided with adequate permanent ventilation in 
accordance with current standards. 
The adequacy of ventilation has not been assessed during this inspection. 
Boiler Flues 
Where a heating appliance discharges through an external wall or roof, the visible flue 
terminal appears secure, adequately positioned, and free from obvious obstruction. 
The installation has not been tested. 
Defects 
One or more of the following defects were observed: 
• 
cracked fire surround  
• 
damaged hearth  
• 
loose fireplace components  
• 
cracked chimney breast  
• 
distorted fireplace opening  
• 
blocked ventilation  
• 
localised damp staining  
• 
surface deterioration

Dampness 
Localised damp staining was observed to the chimney breast.

penetration. 
The source should be identified and repaired before internal redecoration is undertaken. 
General Maintenance 
Fireplaces, flues and combustion appliances should be inspected and serviced regularly by 
appropriately qualified contractors. 
Unused flues should be adequately ventilated to reduce the risk of condensation and 
dampness. 
Where fireplaces are no longer required, appropriate capping and ventilation should be 
maintained.

Utility Room

Bedroom Furniture 
The property incorporates built-in wardrobes, storage cupboards, shelving, or other fitted 
furniture. 
Where visible, these appear in good, reasonable, fair, poor, or very poor condition.

Moisture 
No visible evidence of moisture was observed around the accessible kitchen units. 
or 
Localised moisture staining or deterioration was observed to the units or surrounding 
finishes.

Defects

damaged cupboard doors  
• 
loose hinges

damaged worktops

worn finishes

defective sealant

cracked wall tiles

damaged plinths

water-damaged units

misaligned drawers

loose handles
